title: Battle of Blue Licks
summary: In August 1782 Kentucky militia chasing Caldwell's rangers and their mainly Wyandot and Great Lakes allies were ambushed at Blue Licks; 60 to 77 died.
bodyMarkdown:
On August 19, 1782, about 182 Kentucky militia chasing William Caldwell's raiders were ambushed on a Licking River ridge in today's Robertson County. Caldwell commanded about 50 Butler's Rangers and Detroit Indian Department men alongside a few hundred warriors, mainly Wyandot and Great Lakes warriors, with a few Shawnee, Delaware and Mingo men, according to Capt. Alexander McKee's report to Detroit of August 28, 1782 ([Michigan Pioneer and Historical Collections, vol. 20, pp. 49–50](https://archive.org/details/michiganhistoric20mich_0)). Col. John Todd, Lt. Col. Stephen Trigg and Daniel Boone's son Israel were among the dead.

The force had gathered to meet what proved a false alarm that George Rogers Clark was marching on the Shawnee towns, and most of the larger gathering went home. About 300 rangers and warriors then crossed the Ohio. At Bryan's Station they tried to draw the garrison out: Caldwell wrote that he "tried to draw em out by sending up a small Party," ([Caldwell's report, August 26, 1782](https://www.royalprovincial.com/history/battles/brcald1.shtml)), and McKee that they hoped to "gain some certain Intelligence." No British report describes the attack as a planned diversion to set up Blue Licks.

The raid ran ahead of new orders from Quebec. On August 27, 1782, Maj. Arent DePeyster at Detroit wrote that he had sent word to Caldwell and the other officers "to act on the defensive only," adding, "I fear Capt Caldwell has already passed the Ohio" ([MPHC, vol. 10, pp. 633–634](https://archive.org/details/michiganhistoric10mich)). Interpreters Simon Girty and his brother George were with the force but held no command, according to C. W. Butterfield's [History of the Girtys](https://archive.org/details/historyofgirtysb00butt) (1890).

After the siege of Bryan's Station, Col. John Todd's mounted militia followed Caldwell's trail about 38 miles to the Licking; at the ford Boone warned that the open trail suggested an ambush and urged waiting for Benjamin Logan's reinforcements, but Maj. Hugh McGary's call to attack carried the men across ([American Battlefield Trust](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/blue-licks); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Blue_Licks); see [Hugh McGary](/stories/hugh-mcgary-the-blue-licks-hothead/)). It was the settlers' bloodiest Revolutionary defeat in Kentucky, months after Yorktown: roughly 60 to 77 Kentuckians were killed and several captured. British and Indian losses were light, about 7 to 11 killed; the two British reports differ, and both put the battle a few days later than the American accounts.

For the nations north of the Ohio, the fighting was part of a long defense of homelands and hunting grounds against American settlement, sharpened that year by the Gnadenhutten killings and Crawford's march on the Sandusky towns.

## Kentucky today

The ridge, a stop on the [Licking Valley drive](/drives/licking-valley/), is part of [Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park](https://parks.ky.gov/explore/blue-licks-battlefield-state-resort-park-7782), where a monument lists the Kentucky dead. The [American Battlefield Trust](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/blue-licks) has a battle summary and map.
